title: Italian foundations
description: Thirty-two original A1 foundation lessons (units 1–8). A growing course, not a complete A1 certification syllabus. Adds 17 new CEFR A2 lessons (units 9–13): past tenses, the future, the conditional and courtesy, linking words, and work & technology — including a hotel mission.
attribution: Original VerbaLibera authoring, 2026. MIT. Machine-authored and consistency-checked; native-speaker editorial review remains open. The A2 lessons (units 9–13) are machine-authored and pending native-speaker review.

units.title: Going further
units.objective: Discuss destinations, past actions and plans.

units.title: Time and the world around you
units.objective: Handle days, time, weather and market prices.

units.title: Health and social life
units.objective: Handle aches, the pharmacy, emergencies and invitations.

units.title: In azione
units.objective: Use your Italian in new ways: build sentences, complete a mission, remember what you learned.

units.title: Alla prova
units.objective: Put your Italian to the test: order dinner, find the piazza, build sentences at the bar.

units.title: Il futuro
units.objective: Talk about the future: forming the futuro semplice, promises and predictions, plans and intentions.

units.title: Desideri e cortesia
units.objective: Express wishes and make polite requests with the conditional.

units.title: Collegare le frasi
units.objective: Link ideas: the subjunctive after penso che, ne and ci, relative pronouns, and stare + gerundio.

units.title: Lavoro e tecnologia
units.objective: Compare things, talk about work, and survive a hotel stay — in Italian.

units.title: Il passato
units.objective: Talk about the past: passato prossimo with avere and essere, the imperfetto, and choosing between them.

concepts.title: Names and introductions
concepts.explanation: Io means I. Sono is the I-form of essere (to be). Italian often omits io because the verb identifies the speaker. Use sono with your name or nationality. Ciao is informal; buongiorno is a polite greeting.
concepts.commonError: With io, use sono, not è.

concepts.title: People and essere
concepts.explanation: Tu means you (one familiar person); lui and lei mean he and she. Essere changes: io sono, tu sei, lui/lei è. Use the accent on è (is): e without the accent means and.
concepts.commonError: With tu, essere is sei.

concepts.title: Family and avere
concepts.explanation: Avere means to have: io ho, tu hai, lui/lei ha. The h is silent but required. Un is an indefinite article with a masculine noun; una is feminine. Learn un fratello and una sorella as phrases.
concepts.commonError: With io, avere is ho. The h is silent.

concepts.title: Numbers and age
concepts.explanation: Italian expresses age with avere: ho venti anni literally means I have twenty years. Learn venti (twenty) and trenta (thirty). Hai asks about your age when the voice rises; writing adds a question mark.
concepts.commonError: Use avere for a person’s age: Ho venti anni.

concepts.title: Home and definite articles
concepts.explanation: Il means the with many masculine singular nouns; la with feminine singular nouns. Before a vowel both may become l’. Here casa is feminine and libro is masculine. In una casa means in a house.
concepts.commonError: Libro is masculine: il libro.

concepts.title: Colors and agreement
concepts.explanation: Many adjectives change -o to -a with feminine nouns. A white book is un libro bianco; a white house is una casa bianca. Grande works with either gender. These adjectives normally follow the noun.
concepts.commonError: Casa is feminine, so bianco becomes bianca.

concepts.title: More than one
concepts.explanation: Common masculine nouns change -o to -i: libro → libri. Many feminine nouns change -a to -e: casa → case. The articles also change: il → i; la → le. Sono means are with plural subjects as well as am with io.
concepts.commonError: Plural libri needs plural bianchi.

concepts.title: Study and work
concepts.explanation: Regular -are verbs replace -are with -o for io and -i for tu. Studiare → studio, studi. Lavorare → lavoro, lavori. Ogni giorno means every day. No extra helping verb is needed for I am studying in this context.
concepts.commonError: With io, studiare becomes studio.

concepts.title: Saying no and asking
concepts.explanation: Put non immediately before the verb to negate it: non studio. Do not add an equivalent of English do. A statement can become a yes/no question with intonation and a question mark. Keep subject and verb agreement.

examples.meaning: I do not work at home.

concepts.commonError: The verb still agrees with io: non lavoro.

concepts.title: Food and -ere verbs
concepts.explanation: Regular -ere verbs commonly use -o for io and -i for tu: prendere → prendo, prendi. In a café, prendo un caffè can mean I will have a coffee. Keep the accents on caffè and tè. Acqua is feminine: un’acqua.
concepts.commonError: With io, prendere becomes prendo.

concepts.title: What belongs to whom
concepts.explanation: Possessives agree with the thing owned: il mio libro, la mia casa, i miei libri. The owner’s gender does not determine mio or mia. Ordinary nouns usually keep the article before the possessive.
concepts.commonError: Mia agrees with feminine casa.

concepts.title: Going places
concepts.explanation: Andare is irregular: io vado, tu vai. Use a with cities, and combine a + la as alla, a + il as al. Vado alla stazione means I am going to the station. A Roma has no article.

examples.meaning: I am going to the station.

concepts.commonError: A + la contracts to alla.

concepts.title: Modal verbs and requests
concepts.explanation: Potere means can or be able to: io posso, tu puoi. Follow it with an infinitive: posso prendere. Do not conjugate both verbs. Per favore means please. Vorrei is a useful fixed polite request meaning I would like.
concepts.commonError: After posso, use the infinitive prendere.

concepts.title: Morning routines
concepts.explanation: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun referring back to the subject. Alzarsi means to get up: io mi alzo, tu ti alzi. Mi and ti go before the finite verb. Alle sette means at seven o’clock; alle combines a + le.

examples.meaning: Do you get up at seven?

concepts.commonError: For your own routine with io, use mi alzo.

concepts.title: A first look at the past
concepts.explanation: The passato prossimo combines an auxiliary and a past participle. With mangiare, use avere: ho mangiato. Regular -are participles end in -ato. Ieri means yesterday. This lesson introduces only the I-form with avere.
concepts.commonError: With io, avere is ho: Io ho mangiato.

concepts.title: Tomorrow and future plans
concepts.explanation: Italian often uses the present with a future time expression: domani vado a Roma. Domani makes the time clear. This is a first way to express plans before learning the future tense. Keep the irregular forms vado and vai.

examples.meaning: Tomorrow I am going to Rome.
Are you studying at home tomorrow?

concepts.commonError: Io uses vado, even when the plan is for tomorrow.

concepts.title: Days and dates
concepts.explanation: Italian days and months are masculine and written lowercase: lunedì, maggio. Give the date with the number, di and the month: il tre maggio. Oggi, domani and ieri frame any plan.

examples.target: Il compleanno è il tre maggio.

concepts.commonError: Days of the week are lowercase in Italian: lunedì.

concepts.title: Telling the time
concepts.explanation: Ask the time with Che ore sono? Answer È l’una for one o’clock and Sono le plus the number otherwise: Sono le tre. Add e mezza for half past, e un quarto for quarter past and meno un quarto for quarter to.
concepts.commonError: Hours take sono; only one o’clock takes è: Sono le tre.

concepts.title: Weather and seasons
concepts.explanation: Describe the weather with fa plus an adjective: fa caldo for hot, fa freddo for cold. Say c’è il sole for sunny and piove for it rains. Two seasons to know now are l’estate (summer) and l’inverno (winter).
concepts.commonError: Weather uses fare, not essere: Oggi fa freddo.

concepts.title: Market prices
concepts.explanation: Ask the price with Quanto costa? for one thing and Quanto costano? for several: Quanto costa un chilo di mele? Answer with the price: Tre euro. Un chilo is one kilo and il mercato is the market.

examples.target: Quanto costa un chilo di mele?
examples.meaning: How much is a kilo of apples?

concepts.commonError: Un chilo is singular, so the question is singular: Quanto costa un chilo di mele?

concepts.title: Saying where it hurts
concepts.explanation: Say pain with mi fa male plus the body part: Mi fa male la testa. Headache is il mal di testa and fever is la febbre. Answer Dove fa male? (Where does it hurt?) with Mi fa male plus the spot.
concepts.commonError: Pain uses fare, not essere: Mi fa male la testa.

concepts.title: Asking for medicine
concepts.explanation: Ask for medicine with Ho bisogno di…: Ho bisogno di una medicina. Una pastiglia is a pill and lo sciroppo is syrup. Ask the price with Quanto costa?: Costa cinque euro.
concepts.commonError: Bisogno needs di before the noun: Ho bisogno di una medicina.

concepts.title: Calling for help
concepts.explanation: Call for help with Aiuto! Ask for an ambulance with Chiami un’ambulanza! The emergency number is il centododici (112). Say È urgente when it is urgent.
concepts.commonError: Chiami is the polite command form: Chiami un’ambulanza!

concepts.title: Inviting and replying
concepts.explanation: Invite with Vuoi venire…?: Vuoi venire a cena? Accept with Sì, grazie, volentieri. Decline politely with Mi dispiace, non posso.

examples.meaning: Do you want to come to dinner Saturday?

concepts.commonError: Venire means to come: Vuoi venire a cena?

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Italian grew where Latin was spoken, and thousands of everyday words came into both Italian and English from Latin — nazione, informazione, ristorante, caffè. You can already recognize them before you speak a word of Italian. The words below are the first ones to say out loud: ciao greets friends a dozen times a day, grazie answers kindness, sì and no steer it.
concepts.commonError: Say ciao or buongiorno the moment you arrive — Italians notice warmth more than accent. Ciao is for friends and informal moments; buongiorno opens everything else.

concepts.title: Ordering and paying at a café
concepts.explanation: Order politely with Vorrei un caffè, per favore. Ask the price with Quanto costa? and thank the server with Grazie.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.

concepts.commonError: Use vorrei for a polite request; avoid the direct command Prendo when speaking to the server.

concepts.title: Forming the futuro semplice
concepts.explanation: Italian builds the future from the infinitive itself: drop the final -e and add -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno — parlerò, leggerai, dormirà, partiremo. Watch out: -are verbs change their a to e, so parlare gives parlerò (not *parlarò). A few verbs have short irregular stems to memorize: essere gives sarò, avere gives avrò, andare gives andrò, fare gives farò, potere gives potrò, dovere gives dovrò, sapere gives saprò. Notice the pattern first: every future ending carries the stress — ò, ai, à — it sounds like pointing forward.

examples.meaning: It will be a beautiful day.

concepts.commonError: The -a- of -are verbs becomes -e- in the future: parlare gives parlerò, not *parlarò.

concepts.title: Three jobs of the futuro semplice
concepts.explanation: The futuro semplice does three jobs. First, promises and intentions: Ti prometto, arriverò in tempo — I promise I will arrive on time. Second, predictions: Domani pioverà — it will rain tomorrow. Third, the sneaky one: supposition about the present — Saranno le otto (it must be eight o’clock); Avrà trent’anni (he must be thirty). Same form, three meanings; context tells you which. Notice: Italians guess the present with the future tense.

examples.meaning: I will help you, I promise.

examples.target: Dove sarà Marco? Sarà a casa.
examples.meaning: Where can Marco be? He must be at home.
How old must he be? He must be forty.

concepts.commonError: “Sarà a casa” does not always mean “he will be home” — answering a question about now, the future expresses a guess: he must be home.

concepts.title: Expressing plans without the future tense
concepts.explanation: Italians often express the near future without the futuro tense, using a present plus a planning phrase: Vado a studiare (I am going to study); Penso di cambiare lavoro (I am planning to change jobs); Ho intenzione di partire (I intend to leave); Spero di trovare (I hope to find). The pattern is: planning verb + a/di + infinitive. andare takes a; pensare, sperare and avere intenzione take di. The planning phrase carries the intention; the infinitive carries the action. For timetabled events the plain present does the job: Domani parto alle otto.

examples.meaning: I am going to look for work.
We are planning to move to Milan.

examples.target: Ho intenzione di studiare di più.

examples.meaning: I hope to see you soon.

concepts.commonError: The preposition matters: vado A fare, but penso DI fare. Mixing them — *penso a fare — is the classic slip.

concepts.title: The conditional: the tense of “would”
concepts.explanation: The conditional is the tense of “would”: wishes, dreams, polite hypotheticals. It uses the same stems as the future — parler-, sar-, avr-, andr-, far- — but softer endings: -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero. parlerei, saresti, farebbe — hear how the stress falls back, like a sigh. The irregular stems are the same ones you learned for the futuro: sarei, avrei, andrei, farei, potrei, dovrei, saprei, vorrei. Use it for wishes (vorrei viaggiare), hypotheticals (al tuo posto resterei) and softening (mi piacerebbe). The pattern: future stem plus conditional ending means “would”.

examples.meaning: I would like to travel more.
I would buy a house by the sea.

examples.target: Al tuo posto, non lo farei.
examples.meaning: In your place, I would not do it.
I would like to meet you.

concepts.commonError: Do not confuse future and conditional endings: parlerò means “I will speak”, parlerei means “I would speak”. One vowel changes the whole meaning.

concepts.title: The conditional of courtesy
concepts.explanation: Politeness in Italian is conditional. The present (voglio, puoi) sounds like a demand; the conditional (vorrei, potrebbe) sounds like a request. The magic trio: vorrei (I would like), potrebbe…? (could you…?), sarebbe possibile…? (would it be possible…?). Add mi scusi and per favore and every door opens. Notice the pattern: the softer the verb form, the politer the request. Italians almost never say “voglio” in a shop — it is always “vorrei”.

examples.meaning: I would like a single room.
Would it be possible to have the menu?
Excuse me, could you help me?

concepts.commonError: “Voglio una pizza” in a restaurant sounds rude — always say “vorrei”. The conditional is not optional here; it is the price of politeness.

concepts.title: Vorrei in negozio
concepts.explanation: In shops the conditional runs the whole interaction: vorrei provare (I would like to try) to open, potrebbe dirmi il prezzo (could you tell me the price) to ask, la prendo (I will take it) to close. The pattern: open soft with vorrei, ask with potrebbe, decide with the present. And when you want nothing, the magic phrase is “Sto solo guardando, grazie” — I am just looking, thanks.

examples.meaning: I would like to try on this sweater.
Could you tell me the price?

concepts.commonError: “Voglio provare” sounds demanding in a shop — it is always “vorrei provare”.

concepts.title: The subjunctive after “che”
concepts.explanation: The congiuntivo is the mood of subjectivity — opinions, wishes, doubts. After penso che, credo che, spero che, è importante che and bisogna che, the verb bends: -are verbs take -i endings (parli, mangi), -ere and -ire verbs take -a endings (prenda, parta, finisca). Penso che Maria parli bene; credo che venga domani. The pattern: che plus a subjective trigger means the verb bends. At A2, recognizing penso che plus the subjunctive and producing the common forms is exactly right.

examples.target: Penso che sia una buona idea.
examples.meaning: I think it is a good idea.
I believe he is coming tomorrow.
I hope the weather is nice.
It is important that you study.

concepts.commonError: After “penso che” the indicative is wrong: *penso che è bello must be penso che sia bello. The che triggers the subjunctive.

concepts.title: Ne and ci
concepts.explanation: Two tiny words do heavy lifting. NE replaces “di plus something”: Quanti caffè prendi? Ne prendo due (two of them); Hai parlato del film? Ne abbiamo parlato (we talked about it). CI has three jobs: “there” with essere — c’è, ci sono; “there” of place — ci vado (I am going there), ci vivo; and with verbs like pensare and riuscire — ci penso (I will think about it), non ci riesco (I cannot manage it). The pattern: ne means of-it/of-them; ci means there or about-it. They sit before the verb, just like other pronouns: ne ho due, ci vado.

examples.target: Quante lingue parli? Ne parlo tre.
examples.meaning: How many languages do you speak? I speak three (of them).
I will take care of it.

concepts.commonError: Ne and ci go BEFORE the verb: ne parlo, ci vado — never *parlo ne.

concepts.title: Relative pronouns che and cui
concepts.explanation: Relative pronouns glue two sentences into one. CHE is the workhorse — for people and things, subject or object: il ragazzo che parla (the boy who speaks); il libro che ho comprato (the book I bought). CUI appears after a preposition: la persona A CUI parlo (the person I am talking to); il film DI CUI parli (the film you are talking about); l’amico CON CUI esco (the friend I go out with). The pattern: no preposition means che; a preposition means cui. That is the whole system.

examples.target: Il ragazzo che vedi è mio fratello.
examples.meaning: The boy (who/that) you see is my brother.

examples.target: Il libro che ho letto è bello.
examples.meaning: The book (that) I read is nice.

examples.target: La persona a cui penso sei tu.
examples.meaning: The person I am thinking of is you.

examples.target: Il ristorante di cui parli è chiuso.
examples.meaning: The restaurant you are talking about is closed.

concepts.commonError: After a preposition, che is wrong: *la persona a che parlo must be la persona a cui parlo.

concepts.title: Stare + gerundio for actions in progress
concepts.explanation: For “right now” actions, Italians use stare plus the gerundio: sto mangiando (I am eating); stai dormendo (you are sleeping); stanno guardando (they are watching). The gerundio is easy: -are gives -ando (parlando), -ere and -ire give -endo (leggendo, dormendo), with a few irregulars — facendo, dicendo, bevendo. Stare itself is irregular: sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno. Use it only for actions happening right now — never for habits (*ogni giorno sto leggendo is wrong). The pattern: stare (conjugated) plus the gerundio means “in progress”.

examples.meaning: We are waiting for the bus.
It has been raining for an hour.

concepts.commonError: Stare plus the gerundio is only for right-now: *di solito sto leggendo is wrong — habits use the present or the imperfetto: di solito leggo.

concepts.title: Comparatives: più, meno, and the irregulars
concepts.explanation: Comparing in Italian is formulaic: più plus the adjective plus di — Marco è più alto di me; meno plus the adjective plus di; così… come or tanto… quanto for equality — è alto come me. Use che before a clause or a second adjective: è più intelligente che simpatico; preferisco il treno che l’aereo. A few adjectives have special comparative forms worth memorizing: buono gives migliore, cattivo gives peggiore, grande gives maggiore, piccolo gives minore. The pattern: più/meno… di compares two nouns; più… che introduces a clause.

examples.target: Il treno è più veloce dell’autobus.
examples.meaning: The train is faster than the bus.

examples.target: Questo computer è meno caro di quello.
examples.meaning: This computer is less expensive than that one.

examples.target: Mia sorella è alta come me.
examples.meaning: My sister is as tall as me.

examples.target: Questo vino è migliore di quello.
examples.meaning: This wine is better than that one.

concepts.commonError: Do not double the comparative: *più migliore is wrong — migliore already means “better”. Say più buono or migliore, never both.

concepts.title: The si impersonale: “one does”
concepts.explanation: The si impersonale lets you speak generally — “one does”, “people do”: si lavora (one works); si mangia bene qui (the food is good here, literally “one eats well here”); in Italia si beve molto caffè. Form it with si plus the third person singular: si parla, si dice. It is how Italians state general truths, rules and customs without pointing at anyone. The pattern: si plus the verb means “people in general”. Pair it with this lesson’s work vocabulary and you can discuss any workplace.

examples.target: In questo ufficio si lavora bene.
examples.meaning: One works well in this office.
In Italy people have lunch late.

concepts.commonError: The si impersonale uses the third person singular: si lavora, not *si lavorano. (The plural si with plural objects is beyond A2.)

concepts.title: In albergo: chiedere e risolvere
concepts.explanation: A hotel stay is a chain of polite requests: ho una prenotazione (stating your business), vorrei and potrebbe (asking), non funziona (reporting a problem), è andato tutto benissimo (closing happy). The pattern: state, ask politely, fix, thank. The conditional keeps every request smooth.

examples.target: Ho una prenotazione a nome Rossi.
examples.meaning: I have a reservation under Rossi.

examples.target: Potrebbe darmi un asciugamano in più?
examples.meaning: Could you give me an extra towel?

concepts.commonError: Report problems with “non funziona” (it doesn’t work) — not *non va bene, which sounds like a complaint about quality.

concepts.title: Passato prossimo with avere
concepts.explanation: Italians build the past the way they build a sandwich: a little helper word plus the main verb changed. The helper for most verbs is a form of avere — ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno — and the main verb takes a fixed ending: -are becomes -ato, -ere becomes -uto, -ire becomes -ito. Notice the rhythm first: ho mangiato, hai comprato, abbiamo visto. The pattern is always helper + the -to form. Once you feel it — ho parlato, ho bevuto, ho dormito — the few irregulars (fatto, detto, scritto, visto) are just words to memorize.
concepts.commonError: Never put the infinitive after the helper: it is ho mangiato, not *ho mangiare.

concepts.title: Passato prossimo with essere
concepts.explanation: Not all verbs take avere. Verbs of going, coming, arriving and leaving — movement and change of state — take essere instead: sono andato, sei venuta, siamo partiti. And with essere there is a twist: the participle behaves like an adjective and agrees with the subject. Marco è andato, Maria è andata, i ragazzi sono andati, le ragazze sono andate. The pattern: essere + a participle that matches who did it. A handy memory hook: the movement verbs — andare, venire, arrivare, partire, tornare, entrare, uscire, rimanere, nascere — take essere.

examples.target: Le ragazze sono tornate a casa.

concepts.commonError: With essere the participle must agree: *Maria è andato is wrong — it is Maria è andata.

concepts.title: L’imperfetto: habits and background
concepts.explanation: The imperfetto is the storyteller’s tense: what things were like, what people used to do. Formation is almost boringly regular — take the verb stem and add -avo, -avi, -ava, -avamo, -avate, -avano: parlavo, leggevo, dormivo. Only a few rebels: essere gives ero, fare gives facevo, bere gives bevevo, dire gives dicevo. Use it for repeated actions (ogni giorno giocavo), descriptions (era bello) and ongoing scenes (mentre dormivo). The pattern: the imperfetto paints the background; the passato prossimo reports the events.

examples.meaning: As a child I used to play football.
Every summer we used to go to the seaside.
While I was studying, I listened to music.

concepts.commonError: Do not use the passato prossimo for habits: *ogni giorno ho giocato sounds like a single event — use giocavo.

concepts.title: Choosing between the two past tenses
concepts.explanation: Two past tenses, two jobs. The passato prossimo reports what happened, once, done: ieri ho visto Maria; all’improvviso è partito. The imperfetto paints the background: what was happening, what things were like, what people used to do — mentre camminavo; pioveva; di solito cenavo alle otto. Signal words are your friends: ieri, all’improvviso, poi, alla fine point to the passato prossimo; mentre, ogni giorno, di solito, da bambino point to the imperfetto. The classic scene: Mentre preparavo la cena (background, imperfetto), ha telefonato Marco (event, passato prossimo).

examples.meaning: While I was walking, I saw Maria.

examples.target: Ieri ha piovuto tutto il giorno.

concepts.commonError: Mentre plus a completed action is the classic mistake: *mentre ho camminato is wrong — the ongoing action needs the imperfetto: mentre camminavo.

vocabulary.example: Sono le tre meno un quarto.
La prossima settimana lavorerò da casa.

vocabulary.meaning: I could, I would be able to

vocabulary.example: Di biscotti? Ne ho due, grazie.
Ci penserò e ti farò sapere.
Dov’è Marco? Non ne ho idea.
L’amico a cui scrivo vive a Londra.
Il film di cui parli è famoso.
La ragazza con cui esco è simpatica.
Il motivo per cui chiamo è importante.
La signora, la quale sorride, è mia zia.
In questo momento non posso parlare.
Mi dispiace, sto uscendo proprio ora.
Ho fatto domanda per quel posto.
Ho una prenotazione per due notti.
Qual è la password del wifi?
Ieri ho lavorato fino a tardi.
Ieri sera ho mangiato al ristorante.
Maria ha comprato un libro nuovo.
Sono andato al lavoro in bici.
Una volta ho visto il mare d’inverno.

activities.body: It is 10 a.m. at a Roman bar. The barista is serving quick coffees at the counter. Start with Buongiorno, ask for un caffè, and thank them when they hand it over. In this setting, a caffè is a small espresso.

activities.prompt: At the bar counter, the barista looks up. What is a polite morning greeting?
hints: It's morning and the barista doesn't know you, so the polite daytime greeting is buongiorno. Ciao is for friends, arrivederci is for leaving, and grazie is for thanking.
activities.feedback: Buongiorno suits a morning greeting to someone you do not know.

activities.prompt: Build the order: A coffee, please.
hints: Put the polite request in order: the article un, then the drink caffè, then per favore at the end.
activities.feedback: Un caffè, per favore. This asks for one coffee politely.

activities.prompt: The barista hands you the cup. What do you say?
hints: The barista just handed you the coffee — the word for thanking is grazie. Ciao is a greeting, per favore asks for something, sì means yes.
activities.feedback: Grazie closes the exchange.

activities.prompt: Say the order once in your head. Then write in Italian: A coffee, please.
hints: Write the order you built with the tiles: un + caffè (with the accent on the è) + per favore.
activities.feedback: You wrote the order without the tiles.

errors.explanation: caffè is written with a grave accent on the è — caffe would be read differently in Italian.
Caffè is a masculine noun, so it takes un: un caffè, not una.
Vorrei (I would like) is the more polite order you'll meet in a later lesson. This mission teaches the simple order: Un caffè, per favore.

activities.prompt: Match the three lines you used to their meanings.
hints: Match each line you used to its English meaning: buongiorno is the hello, the coffee line is the request, grazie is the thanks.
activities.feedback: You can recognize the whole exchange.

activities.prompt: Write the three lines in order: Good morning. / A coffee, please. / Thank you.
hints: Three lines in exchange order: the morning greeting, then the coffee request, then the thanks — each line ends with a period.
activities.feedback: You greeted the barista, ordered, and thanked them.

answers: Buongiorno. Un caffè, per favore. Grazie.

errors.explanation: At the bar you don't know the barista, so use the polite Buongiorno, not the informal ciao.

errors.answer: Buongiorno. Grazie. Un caffè, per favore.
errors.explanation: The English dictates the exchange order: greet first (Buongiorno), then the order, then the thanks.

activities.body: Today you are the builder, not the reader. You already know every word in this lesson — vorrei, prendo, posso, un caffè, per favore. Your job is to snap the tiles into the right order. Look at the three model sentences above. Notice how the polite words sit at the edges and the verb comes first. Think about the shape, then build.

activities.prompt: Think about the model, then build: I would like a coffee, please.
activities.feedback: Vorrei opens a polite request, then the thing you want, then per favore to close it. The comma before per favore is the written breath of politeness.

activities.prompt: Build: I will have a tea.
activities.feedback: Prendo is io + prendere: in a café it means “I'll have”. Un tè keeps its accent — tè, not te.

activities.prompt: Which of these is a correct Italian word order?
activities.feedback: The verb of wanting comes first: vorrei + the thing. Italian doesn't front the object the way the wrong options do.

activities.prompt: Complete the order. Think: which little word sits between vorrei and caffè?
activities.feedback: Un caffè — masculine, so un. You met this exact sentence in «At the café: order and pay»: Vorrei un caffè, per favore.

activities.prompt: Build: Can I have a coffee? (use potere + the infinitive)
activities.feedback: Posso + infinitive: potere always leans on another verb. Posso prendere — “can I take”, the polite café ask.

activities.prompt: Complete it: ___ un tè, per favore.
activities.feedback: Prendo — the io form. Prendi would be talking to the other person, not ordering for yourself.

activities.prompt: Now without tiles. Write in Italian: I would like a tea, please.
activities.feedback: Vorrei un tè, per favore. Same frame as the coffee — only the drink changed. That's the power of a pattern.

activities.prompt: Final build — the whole table's order: I would like a coffee and a tea, please.
activities.feedback: One frame, two drinks: vorrei … e … per favore. You just built a real café sentence from nothing but tiles.

activities.body: Costruisci: al bar. In this lesson you build every sentence yourself, tile by tile. Notice first, then think, then try: the verb changes with the person — prendo for io, prendi for tu — while vorrei never changes and is always polite. Look at the three models above: find the verb in each, say who it belongs to, then start building.

activities.prompt: Build: I'll have a coffee.
activities.feedback: Io + prendere → prendo, then un caffè. The accent on caffè is part of the word — never drop it.

activities.prompt: Build: Will you have a tea?
activities.feedback: Tu + prendere → prendi, and the question mark turns the statement into an offer. Compare with the tile you just built: one letter changes the whole person.

activities.prompt: Change your mind politely: «Non ___ un caffè, grazie.»
activities.feedback: Non sits immediately before the verb: non prendo. No extra words, no do — Italian negation is one small word in exactly the right place.

activities.prompt: Build: I would like a tea, please.
activities.feedback: Vorrei never changes — io, tu, always vorrei. Then the thing, then per favore: the polite frame you can reuse anywhere.

activities.prompt: The barista asks: «Cosa prendi?» Which answer is correct for you?
activities.feedback: Cosa prendi? asks YOU (tu → prendi), but the answer flips to io → prendo. The third option leaves the verb unconjugated — prendere alone is never a finished answer.

activities.prompt: Build: The coffee is hot.
activities.feedback: È with the accent means is — e without it means and. And caldo matches caffè: masculine singular, like bianco with il libro.

activities.prompt: Careful — the tea is cold: «Il tè ___ freddo.»
activities.feedback: È, with the accent. This tiny mark is the whole difference between is and and — Italian spelling carries meaning.

activities.prompt: Type the full polite refusal: I won't have a tea, thanks.
activities.feedback: Non prendo un tè, grazie — negation, verb, thing, politeness, all in one breath. You built this from tiles; now it lives in your head.

activities.body: Italian builds the future from the infinitive itself: parlare gives parlerò, leggere gives leggerò, dormire gives dormirò. Feel the endings — ò, ai, à, emo, ete, anno — always stressed, always leaning forward. Read the examples and notice how the -a- of -are verbs quietly becomes -e-.

activities.prompt: Domani ___ a Roma. (andare — I will go)
activities.feedback: andare is irregular in the future: andrò. vado is present (fine for near plans, but this exercise wants the future form); sono andato is past; andrei is the conditional — coming in the next unit.

activities.prompt: Type: They will eat together. (mangiare)
activities.feedback: mangiare gives the stem manger- plus -anno: mangeranno.

activities.prompt: Non lo so: ___ domani. (sapere — I will know)
activities.feedback: sapere has the irregular stem sapr-: saprò. so is present; ho saputo is past; saprei is conditional.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Next week we will work from home.
activities.feedback: Time phrase first, then the future verb: La prossima settimana lavoreremo da casa.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: essere is irregular: sarò. “Fra due giorni” points to the future.

activities.body: Plans do not always need the future tense. Vado a fare, penso di fare, ho intenzione di fare — intention plus infinitive. Notice the little prepositions: andare takes A, pensare and friends take DI. Read the examples and hear how naturally Italians stack a plan onto an infinitive.

activities.prompt: ___ di cambiare lavoro quest’anno. (I intend…)
hints: The fixed phrase for 'I intend to' is avere intenzione di — so 'I intend' is ho intenzione. The other options sound alike but aren't real forms: intenzione is a noun.
activities.feedback: The fixed phrase is avere intenzione di plus the infinitive. The others are invented forms — intenzione is a noun, not a verb.

activities.prompt: Type: We are going to travel in August. (viaggiare)
hints: The near future again with a new verb: andiamo a viaggiare — andare + a + infinitive, and ad before agosto, which starts with a vowel.
activities.feedback: andare a plus the infinitive is the near future: andiamo a viaggiare.

errors.explanation: The near future needs a before the infinitive: andiamo a viaggiare ad agosto.
The subject is we, so the verb is conjugated: andiamo, not the infinitive andare.
After a comes the INFINITIVE viaggiare, not the noun viaggio: andiamo a viaggiare.

activities.prompt: Spero ___ trovare un buon hotel. (to find)
hints: sperare takes di before the infinitive: spero di trovare. Not a (that's for andare) and not che (that starts a clause with its own subject).
activities.feedback: sperare takes di before the infinitive: spero di trovare.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: We are planning to move to Milan.
hints: pensare takes di before the infinitive: pensiamo di trasferirci — then the destination, a Milano.
activities.feedback: pensare takes DI before the infinitive: Pensiamo di trasferirci a Milano.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
hints: The near future with andare: the noi form andiamo, then a, then the infinitive — andiamo a visitare.
activities.feedback: The near future with andare: andiamo a visitare — we are going to visit.

errors.explanation: The near future needs the full bridge: andiamo A visitare — andare takes a before the infinitive.
The sentence needs a conjugated verb: andiamo a visitare. The bare infinitive can't carry the subject.
The subject is noi — this summer, we: andiamo, not vado (io).

activities.body: “Would.” The softest word in Italian grammar. The conditional takes the future’s stems — parler-, sar-, andr- — and gives them gentle endings: -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero. Read the examples and feel the difference: parlerò (I will, firm) versus parlerei (I would, dreaming).

activities.prompt: ___ viaggiare di più quest’anno. (I would like…)
activities.feedback: A wish takes the conditional: mi piacerebbe. mi piace is a present fact; mi piacerà is future; mi è piaciuto is past.

activities.prompt: Type: I would buy a house. (comprare)
activities.feedback: comprare gives the stem comprer- plus -ei: comprerei.

activities.prompt: ___ aiutarti, ma sono occupato. (potere — I could)
activities.feedback: potere is irregular: potrei. A hypothetical ability takes the conditional.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: In your place, I would stay home.
activities.feedback: The hypothetical frame first (al tuo posto), then the conditional: resterei.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: dovere is irregular: dovrei — “I should”.

activities.body: In Italy, politeness has a tense: the conditional. Voglio demands; vorrei requests. Puoi orders; potrebbe asks. Read the four model phrases — vorrei, potrebbe, sarebbe possibile, mi scusi — and notice how every one of them leans back softly instead of pushing forward.

activities.prompt: ___ dirmi l’ora, per favore? (Could you tell me…)
activities.feedback: A polite request to a stranger takes the conditional: potrebbe. può is blunt; poteva is past; potrà is future.

activities.prompt: Type politely: I would like a single room.
activities.feedback: volere gives vorrei. In hotels and shops, vorrei is the only correct choice.

activities.prompt: ___ possibile avere il menù? (Would it be…)
activities.feedback: The fixed polite phrase is “sarebbe possibile”.

activities.prompt: Make it polite: Dammi il conto.
activities.feedback: “Dammi” is an order; the conditional plus the indirect pronoun turns it into a polite request.

activities.body: You are in a clothes shop in Milan. Your tools: vorrei to ask softly, potrebbe for questions, la prendo to buy, and “sto solo guardando” to escape. Read the four model exchanges above — then it is your turn at the counter.

activities.prompt: Vorrei ___ questa maglia. (to try on)
activities.feedback: After vorrei comes the infinitive: vorrei provare. provo is present, provato is a participle, proverò is future.

activities.prompt: Type: I would like to try these shoes.
activities.feedback: vorrei plus the infinitive provare, then the object: Vorrei provare queste scarpe.

activities.prompt: Avete una taglia più ___? (bigger)
activities.feedback: You need the adjective grande. grandezza is the noun “size”; ingrandire is the verb “to enlarge”; grandioso means “grandiose”.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Where is the fitting room, please?
activities.feedback: Dov’è plus the place, then per favore: Dov’è il camerino, per favore?

activities.prompt: Type: Could you tell me the price?
activities.feedback: The polite question pattern: potrebbe plus the infinitive — potrebbe dirmi il prezzo?

activities.prompt: La maglia è troppo ___. (small)
activities.feedback: maglia is feminine singular, so the adjective is piccola. poco is an adverb; piccolezza is the noun “smallness”; piccolina is a diminutive — cute, but not what you mean here.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: The escape phrase every shopper needs: “Sto solo guardando, grazie” — I am just looking, thanks.

activities.prompt: The sweater fits! Type: I’ll take it. (feminine: la maglia)
activities.feedback: The closing line of every purchase: la prendo — literally “I take it”. Short, friendly, final.

activities.prompt: The assistant asks: “Posso aiutarla?” (Can I help you?) Type your polite reply: you are just looking.
activities.feedback: Transfer: you reused “sto solo guardando, grazie” in a real exchange. That is the whole lesson in one sentence.

activities.body: Welcome to the congiuntivo — the verb mood Italians use for opinions, hopes and doubts. The good news: at A2 you only need the pattern. After penso che, credo che, spero che and è importante che, the verb shifts: -are verbs end in -i (parli), -ere and -ire verbs end in -a (prenda, finisca). Read the examples and watch the verbs bend after che.

activities.prompt: Penso che Maria ___ ragione. (avere — she is right)
activities.feedback: avere gives abbia in the subjunctive. After penso che, ha (indicative) is wrong; avrà is future; avrebbe is conditional.

activities.prompt: Type: I think he speaks well. (parlare)
activities.feedback: parlare gives parli: -are verbs take -i in the subjunctive.

activities.prompt: È importante che tu ___ ogni giorno. (studiare)
activities.feedback: studiare gives studi after è importante che. studia is the indicative — wrong after this trigger.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I believe he is coming tomorrow.
activities.feedback: Trigger (credo che) plus the bent verb (venga): Credo che venga domani.

activities.prompt: Add doubt: È vero. → Non credo che…
activities.feedback: essere gives sia in the subjunctive: non credo che sia vero.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: fare is irregular in the subjunctive: faccia. Spero che faccia bel tempo.

activities.prompt: Secondo il testo, qual è la cosa più difficile? (What is the hardest thing?)
activities.feedback: The text says: “Credo che la cosa più difficile sia il congiuntivo” — with sia in the subjunctive, naturally.

answers: La cosa più difficile è il congiuntivo.

activities.body: Ne and ci: two syllables that unlock fluent Italian. Ne means “of it / of them” — ne prendo due. Ci means “there” — ci vado, ci sono — or “about it” — ci penso. They always hop in front of the verb. Read the examples and notice how much meaning hides in two letters.

activities.prompt: Quanti caffè prendi? — ___ prendo due. (I’ll have two of them)
activities.feedback: Two OF THEM means ne. ci means “there”; li and lo are direct pronouns (them, him) without the “of”.

activities.prompt: Type: Yes, I’m going there. (andare)
activities.feedback: “There” of place is ci: ci vado.

activities.prompt: “Ci sono molti turisti in piazza.” What does “ci sono” mean here?
activities.feedback: ci plus essere means “there is / there are”: ci sono molti turisti = there are many tourists.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I have no idea.
activities.feedback: Non plus ne plus the verb: Non ne ho idea. The little word sits before the verb.

activities.prompt: Complete the answer.
activities.feedback: parlare di plus the thing becomes ne: “del viaggio” is replaced by ne — ne ho parlato ieri.

segments.text: Hai parlato con Marco del viaggio? — Sì,

activities.body: Two sentences, one pronoun: che and cui are the glue. Che does almost everything — il libro che ho letto. Cui steps in after prepositions — a cui, di cui, con cui. Read the examples and watch how two short sentences become one smooth Italian sentence.

activities.prompt: Il ragazzo ___ ho visto ieri è mio cugino. (whom I saw)
activities.feedback: No preposition and a direct object means che. cui needs a preposition (a cui, di cui); chi asks questions; quale needs an article.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: The film you are talking about is beautiful.
activities.feedback: parlare takes DI: di plus cui — Il film di cui parli è bello.

activities.prompt: Join into one sentence: Parlo spesso con Maria. Maria è gentile.
activities.feedback: “con Maria” becomes con cui, and the two sentences merge: Maria, con cui parlo spesso, è gentile.

answers: Maria, con cui parlo spesso, è gentile.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: parlare takes DI: di plus cui — Ecco il libro di cui ti ho parlato.

activities.prompt: Cosa fai? — ___ cucinando. (I’m cooking)
activities.feedback: An action in progress takes stare plus the gerundio: sto cucinando. “Sono cucinando” does not exist; sono plus a participle would be the passato prossimo (sono andato).

activities.prompt: Say it as an action in progress: Leggo un libro.
activities.feedback: Present becomes in-progress: sto leggendo.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: Right now, on the phone: sto guidando — I am driving.

activities.body: Comparisons are equations: più… di, meno… di, così… come. Plug in the adjective and you are done. A few rebels — migliore, peggiore, maggiore, minore — replace the whole equation. Read the examples and spot the pattern before the exceptions.

activities.prompt: Il treno è ___ veloce dell’autobus. (faster)
activities.feedback: Comparing two things takes più… di. molto is just “very”; il più is the superlative; tanto needs quanto.

activities.prompt: Type: My house is bigger than yours.
activities.feedback: più plus grande plus di: più grande della tua.

answers: La mia casa è più grande della tua.

activities.prompt: Questo ristorante è ___ di quello. (better)
activities.feedback: buono gives migliore — an adjective, agreeing with ristorante. “più migliore” is a double comparative, wrong; meglio is the adverb.

activities.prompt: Say it as an equality: È alto. (like me)
activities.feedback: Equality takes così… come — the così is often dropped: alto come me.

activities.prompt: Complete the comparison.
activities.feedback: Two coffees compared: più buono di — “more good than”.

activities.prompt: Secondo il testo, perché ha scelto il secondo computer? (Why the second one?)
activities.feedback: “per il mio lavoro è migliore, perché viaggio molto” — lighter and better for travelling work.

answers: Perché è più leggero e migliore per il suo lavoro.

activities.body: How do you say “people do X” without saying who? With si: si lavora, si parla, si mangia. The si impersonale is Italy’s way of stating how things are done — rules, customs, general truths. The verb stays third person singular; si does the rest.

activities.prompt: In Italia ___ molto caffè. (bere — one drinks)
hints: The si impersonale puts si before a third-person-singular verb: si beve. Si bevi is second person and si bevono is a plural — neither fits 'one drinks'.
activities.feedback: si plus the third person singular: si beve. si bevi is second person — wrong; si bevono would need a plural object; “beve si” puts si in the wrong place.

activities.prompt: ___ dice che pioverà domani. (People say…)
hints: 'People say' is si dice — the impersonal si plus the verb. Ci means 'there', ne 'of it', li 'them': none of them say who does the saying.
activities.feedback: “People say” is si dice. ci means “there”; ne means “of it”; li means “them”.

activities.prompt: Make it impersonal: La gente mangia bene qui.
hints: The impersonal version drops the subject: si + third-person-singular verb takes over — qui si mangia bene.
activities.feedback: “La gente mangia” becomes the impersonal si mangia.

errors.explanation: The si impersonale always keeps the verb singular: si mangia bene, never si mangiano.

errors.answer: Qui la gente si mangia bene.
errors.explanation: The transformation replaces la gente with si — the people can't 'eat themselves'. Keep si impersonale and drop the subject: Qui si mangia bene.
The impersonal sentence needs si: Qui si mangia bene.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
hints: A general truth about the company starts with si: Si parla tre lingue.
activities.feedback: A general truth about the company: Si parla tre lingue.

segments.text: parla tre lingue in questa azienda.

errors.explanation: Ci is a particle meaning there/us — the impersonal subject is si: Si parla tre lingue.
The blank holds only si — parla is already written in the sentence.
Without si the sentence loses its impersonal meaning: Si parla tre lingue.

activities.body: Missione: è sera e arrivi in albergo a Firenze. Il tuo obiettivo è chiaro: fare il check-in, chiedere la password del wifi e l’ora della colazione, risolvere un piccolo problema in camera e ripartire felice. I quattro scambi qui sopra sono i tuoi strumenti: la prenotazione per cominciare, vorrei e potrebbe per chiedere, “non funziona” per i problemi. Leggili una volta, poi tocca a te.

activities.prompt: Arrivi alla reception. Cosa dici per primo?
hints: Open with the greeting that fits the evening and give your reservation: Buonasera, ho una prenotazione a nome… — polite, and it hands them exactly what they need.
activities.feedback: Start with a greeting plus the reservation — polite, and it gives them exactly what they need. “Dammi” is rude; the price and the room location come later.

options.text: Buonasera, ho una prenotazione a nome Rossi.

activities.prompt: Type: I have a reservation under the name Bianchi.
hints: The fixed phrase is a nome + surname: ho una prenotazione a nome Bianchi — the surname follows a nome.
activities.feedback: The fixed phrase is “a nome” plus the surname: a nome Bianchi.

answers: Ho una prenotazione a nome Bianchi.
Io ho una prenotazione a nome Bianchi.

errors.answer: Ho una prenotazione con nome Bianchi.
errors.explanation: The fixed phrase is a nome: a nome Bianchi, not con.
The phrase needs a: ho una prenotazione a nome Bianchi.

activities.prompt: Vuoi la password del wifi. Come chiedi?
hints: Asking for the wifi starts with Qual è (what is): Qual è la password del wifi? The imperative Dammi is rude at a reception desk.
activities.feedback: “Qual è la password del wifi?” is the natural, polite question. The others are rude or ask the wrong thing.

options.text: Qual è la password del wifi?

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: What time is breakfast?
hints: The question frame is a che ora è (at what hour is), then the thing: la colazione — A che ora è la colazione?
activities.feedback: A che ora è…? — the classic question frame, then the thing: la colazione.

activities.prompt: In camera, la doccia non funziona. Type: The shower doesn’t work.
hints: For a broken machine or fixture use non funziona — the shower: La doccia non funziona.
activities.feedback: funzionare means “to work” for machines, showers and wifi: non funziona.

errors.explanation: The shower is the subject (la doccia), so the verb is third person: non funziona. Funziono would be io.
Funzione is the noun 'function' — the verb is funziona: La doccia non funziona.
Negation is non before the verb: non funziona. No is for answering yes/no questions.

activities.prompt: Complete the polite request at the reception.
hints: The polite 'give me' is darmi, and potrebbe carries the courtesy: Potrebbe darmi una camera più tranquilla? — a request, not a demand.
activities.feedback: potrebbe plus darmi — the formal “mi” attached to the infinitive: potrebbe darmi. A polite request, not a demand.

errors.explanation: With potrebbe the pronoun goes on the END of the infinitive: potrebbe darmi — not mi dare.
The pronoun attaches to the end of the infinitive: darmi, not dare mi.
Dammi is the blunt command 'give me' — the polite form is potrebbe darmi.

activities.prompt: Il check-out è ___ mezzogiorno. (at noon)
hints: Times expressed with essere take a: il check-out è a mezzogiorno — a is the preposition for clock moments.
activities.feedback: Time expressions with essere use a: è a mezzogiorno.

activities.prompt: Tutto è andato bene. Type: I’d like the bill — everything was perfect.
hints: Combine the two closing lines: vorrei il conto (the polite request) + è andato tutto benissimo (everything went great).
activities.feedback: Close the mission in style: vorrei il conto plus è andato tutto benissimo. Missione compiuta!

answers: Vorrei il conto, è andato tutto benissimo.
Vorrei il conto, è andato tutto bene.

errors.explanation: The prompt asks for both lines — add that everything went well: è andato tutto benissimo.

errors.answer: Voglio il conto, è andato tutto benissimo.
errors.explanation: Voglio is blunt; the polite request is vorrei (I would like).

errors.answer: Vorrei il conto, è andato tutto meglio.
errors.explanation: Meglio is 'better' — the closing phrase is benissimo (everything went great).

activities.body: You already know the present — mangio, lavoro, dormo. Now you get the past, and it is simpler than it looks: every passato prossimo is just two pieces, a helper (ho, hai, ha…) plus the verb with a -to ending. Read the four examples above and listen for the rhythm: helper + participle. Then you will build your own.

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly says “Yesterday I ate a pizza”?
activities.feedback: The passato prossimo needs two parts: the helper ho plus the past participle mangiato. “Ieri mangio” is present tense — I eat. “Ho mangiare” uses the infinitive, which can never follow the helper. “Mi mangio” is reflexive and means something else entirely.

activities.prompt: You bought a book yesterday. Type: I bought a book.
activities.feedback: comprare gives comprato — regular -are verbs take -ato. The helper for “I” is ho. So: ho + comprato.

activities.prompt: Noi ___ visto il film. (we saw)
activities.feedback: vedere takes avere, and with noi the helper is abbiamo. siamo is the essere-helper — you meet it in the next lesson. ho and ha are singular.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: They called the doctor.
activities.feedback: Helper first (hanno), then the participle (chiamato), then the rest: Hanno chiamato il dottore.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence.
activities.feedback: Maria is third person singular, so the helper is ha. With avere the participle never changes: comprato stays comprato.

activities.prompt: Quick check — match each comparative to its meaning.
activities.feedback: Comparatives locked in. Nice.

activities.body: Your mission: it's 7:40 in the morning at Milano Centrale, and your train to Venice leaves at quarter to eight. Read the departure board, ask the time, and tell your friend when to meet you on the platform. The essentials are below — half past, quarter to, midday. Read each line out loud once, then move.

activities.prompt: The departure board flashes: «Partenza 8:15». A traveler asks what time that is. What do you say?
hints: 8:15 is a quarter PAST eight, so the time is otto e un quarto. Meno un quarto would be 7:45, and only one option pairs the right hour with the right minutes.
activities.feedback: Sono le otto e un quarto — hours first, then the minutes. Meno un quarto would be 7:45.

options.text: Sono le otto e un quarto.
Sono le otto meno un quarto.
Sono le nove e un quarto.

activities.prompt: You call your friend: tell them the train leaves at quarter to eight. Write it in Italian.
hints: Quarter to eight is alle otto meno un quarto. Start with Il treno parte (the train leaves) or just Parte — you're on the phone, so the subject can stay out.
activities.feedback: Il treno parte alle otto meno un quarto. — say it out loud, then run.

answers: Il treno parte alle otto meno un quarto.
Parte alle otto meno un quarto.

errors.answer: Il treno parte alle otto e un quarto.
errors.explanation: e un quarto is quarter PAST the hour (8:15). Quarter to eight is meno un quarto: alle otto meno un quarto.

errors.answer: Il treno parte alle sette meno un quarto.
errors.explanation: Alle sette meno un quarto would be 6:45. Quarter to eight is an hour later: alle otto meno un quarto.

errors.answer: Il treno parte a le otto meno un quarto.
errors.explanation: a + le fuses into alle — a le otto is never written as two words.

activities.prompt: On the platform a fellow traveler asks «Che ore sono?» It's 12:30. What do you answer?
hints: It's half past twelve: the hour is dodici, so the answer is Sono le dodici e mezza — only one o'clock ever takes the singular È.
activities.feedback: Sono le dodici e mezza — with plural hours it's always Sono le. È mezzogiorno is for exactly noon.

activities.prompt: The plan is set. Write in Italian: “We intend to leave on Saturday.”
hints: A firm plan uses avere intenzione di + infinitive: abbiamo intenzione di partire sabato — the noi form of avere, then di, then the infinitive.
activities.feedback: Abbiamo intenzione di partire sabato. — avere intenzione di plus infinitive: the Italian way to state a firm plan.

answers: Abbiamo intenzione di partire di sabato.

errors.explanation: After di the verb is the INFINITIVE: partire. Partiamo would be a second conjugated verb — abbiamo intenzione di partire sabato.
The plan is 'we', so the verb is abbiamo, not ho (io): Abbiamo intenzione di partire sabato.
The phrase needs di before the infinitive: abbiamo intenzione di partire.

activities.prompt: Your friend asks what you hope to do in Rome. Choose the natural reply.
hints: Your hope in Rome: spero di visitare — sperare takes di before the infinitive, never a, and never che (che would need a different subject).
activities.feedback: Spero di visitare — sperare takes di before the infinitive, never a or che (che is for a different subject).

activities.prompt: Build the ad's headline. Say: They are looking for a colleague.
hints: The headline puts the verb first: cercano (they look for), then un collega.
activities.feedback: Cercano un collega. — the headline of half the job ads in Italy.

activities.prompt: Decision made: write in Italian “I applied for the job.”
hints: Applying for a job is fare domanda — in the past: ho fatto domanda per quel posto.
activities.feedback: Ho fatto domanda per quel posto. — fare domanda, literally “to make a request”: how Italians say “apply”.

answers: Ho fatto domanda per quel posto.

errors.answer: Ho fatto domanda per quello posto.
errors.explanation: Before a plain consonant the demonstrative is quel: quel posto, not quello.

errors.answer: Ho fatto domanda per un posto.
errors.explanation: Un posto is 'a position' — the prompt says the specific job: quel posto.
The prompt fixes the past (applied): ho fatto domanda, not faccio.

activities.prompt: An ad says: «Si cerca un cameriere.» What does it mean?
hints: Si cerca means 'one seeks' — the impersonal si hides the who and states the what, so 'they are looking for a waiter'.
activities.feedback: Si cerca — “one seeks”: the si impersonale hides the who and states the what.

options.text: They are looking for a waiter.
The waiter is looking for something.

activities.body: Scene: the waiting room of Dr. Rossi's office in Florence. You woke up with a pounding head and a fever, and today you're the patient. Read the scene once, then step in — the doctor is ready for you.

activities.prompt: The doctor asks «Da quanto tempo?» — since when? What do you answer?
activities.feedback: Da ieri sera — since last night. The doctor needs the timeline before anything else.

activities.prompt: The doctor asks: «Prende medicine?» — do you take any medicine? Choose your reply.
activities.feedback: Una pastiglia al giorno — one pill a day. Clear answers get clear diagnoses.

activities.prompt: The doctor says «Apra la bocca». What is he asking you to do?
activities.feedback: Apra la bocca — open your mouth. Doctors use the formal imperative: apra, not apri.

activities.prompt: The visit is over. Message a friend in Italian: “The doctor says I have a fever.”
activities.feedback: Il dottore dice che ho la febbre. — now go rest.

activities.prompt: It's for your headache. What do you reply?

activities.body: Il vicino bussa alla porta con una scatola. «È per te», dice. Anna spera che sia la scatola dei suoi libri. (The neighbor knocks with a box. Anna hopes it holds her books.)

errors.explanation: È (is) carries the grave accent; e without the accent means and.

Nel pomeriggio Marco lavora in un bar del centro. La sera è stanco, ma torna ai libri per un’ora. L’esame si avvicina. (He works in a downtown café in the afternoon. Tired that evening, he returns to his books for an hour. The exam is getting closer.)

activities.prompt: Where does Marco study in the morning?

activities.feedback: Studia ogni sera. — routine is routine.

errors.explanation: Studiare is the infinitive (to study); with Marco (lui) the form is studia.

activities.body: Lunedì sera Marco chiude il libro: l’esame è finito. Sorride al calendario. Domani può dormire! (On Monday evening, the exam is over. Marco closes his book and smiles at the calendar. Tomorrow he can sleep.)

activities.prompt: Write in Italian: Marco studies and works every day.

activities.body: Sofia va a Roma per il compleanno di suo fratello. Alle otto arriva alla stazione con una valigia rossa e un regalo. (Sofia is going to Rome for her brother’s birthday. She reaches the station at eight with a red suitcase and a gift.)

Il treno è in ritardo. Sofia guarda l’orologio e chiama suo fratello: «Vado a Roma, ma il treno non parte!» (The train is late. Sofia checks the clock and calls her brother: “I’m going to Rome, but the train isn’t leaving!”)

activities.prompt: Write in Italian: On Monday the sun is out.
activities.feedback: Lunedì c’è il sole.

La musicista arriva, ma il cielo si oscura. I bambini stanno giocando a pallone; una donna sta aspettando l’autobus sotto la pensilina. (The musician arrives as the sky darkens. Children are playing ball, and a woman is waiting for the bus under the shelter.)

activities.body: All’improvviso comincia a piovere. Tutti stanno correndo sotto la pensilina, ma la musicista continua a suonare. Marco chiude il giornale e ascolta. (Rain starts suddenly. Everyone runs under the shelter, but the musician keeps playing. Marco closes his paper and listens.)

lessons.objective: Pull words and sentences back from memory — nothing new, just remembering.

lessons.title: Missione: cena in pizzeria
lessons.objective: Order dinner for two at a pizzeria and ask for the bill — in Italian, start to finish.

lessons.title: Missione: trova la piazza
lessons.objective: Ask for directions and find the piazza where your friend is waiting.

lessons.title: Costruisci: al bar
lessons.objective: Build sentences tile by tile: say what you and your friend will have at the bar.

lessons.title: Il futuro semplice
lessons.objective: Form the futuro semplice and talk about tomorrow.
lessons.culturalNote: Italians often use the present for the near future — “domani parto” — but the futuro semplice adds weight: a promise, a set plan, or a guess about the present (which is the next lesson).

lessons.title: Il futuro: promesse e previsioni
lessons.objective: Use the future for promises, predictions and suppositions about the present.
lessons.culturalNote: The supposition future is everywhere in spoken Italian — “Quanto costerà?” (I wonder how much it costs), “Chi sarà?” (who can that be at the door). It makes you sound native fast.

lessons.title: Progetti e intenzioni
lessons.objective: Talk about plans with andare a, pensare di and avere intenzione di.
lessons.culturalNote: Asking “che progetti hai?” (what are your plans) is standard Italian small talk — for the summer, the weekend, life. These phrases are your answer kit.

lessons.title: Il condizionale presente
lessons.objective: Form the conditional and express wishes and hypotheticals.
lessons.culturalNote: The conditional is Italy’s politeness engine — you will hear vorrei, potrebbe and sarebbe possibile dozens of times a day in shops and offices. The next lesson is all about that.

lessons.title: La cortesia: vorrei e potrebbe
lessons.objective: Make polite requests with the conditional: vorrei, potrebbe, sarebbe possibile.
lessons.culturalNote: Service in Italy is a ritual of mutual courtesy: you say “vorrei”, they say “prego”. Using the conditional marks you instantly as someone who gets it.

lessons.title: In negozio: vorrei provare
lessons.objective: Try on clothes and ask politely in a shop — vorrei, potrebbe, la prendo.

lessons.title: Il congiuntivo: penso che…
lessons.objective: Use the present subjunctive after penso che, credo che and spero che.

legacyExercises.prompt: Penso che Maria ___ ragione. (avere — she is right)
legacyExercises.explanation: avere gives abbia in the subjunctive. After penso che, ha (indicative) is wrong; avrà is future; avrebbe is conditional.

legacyExercises.prompt: Type: I think he speaks well. (parlare)
legacyExercises.explanation: parlare gives parli: -are verbs take -i in the subjunctive.

legacyExercises.prompt: È importante che tu ___ ogni giorno. (studiare)
legacyExercises.explanation: studiare gives studi after è importante che. studia is the indicative — wrong after this trigger.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I believe he is coming tomorrow.
legacyExercises.explanation: Trigger (credo che) plus the bent verb (venga): Credo che venga domani.

legacyExercises.prompt: Add doubt: È vero. → Non credo che…
legacyExercises.explanation: essere gives sia in the subjunctive: non credo che sia vero.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
legacyExercises.explanation: fare is irregular in the subjunctive: faccia. Spero che faccia bel tempo.

answers: La cosa più difficile è il congiuntivo.
legacyExercises.prompt: Secondo il testo, qual è la cosa più difficile? (What is the hardest thing?)
legacyExercises.explanation: The text says: “Credo che la cosa più difficile sia il congiuntivo” — with sia in the subjunctive, naturally.
legacyExercises.passage: Secondo me, l’italiano non è difficile, ma penso che sia importante studiare ogni giorno. Credo che la cosa più difficile sia il congiuntivo, perché ha molte forme. Spero che con la pratica diventi più facile. È importante che non abbiate paura di sbagliare: gli errori aiutano a imparare!
legacyExercises.translation: In my opinion, Italian is not difficult, but I think it is important to study every day. I believe the hardest thing is the subjunctive, because it has many forms. I hope it becomes easier with practice. It is important that you are not afraid of making mistakes: mistakes help you learn!

lessons.culturalNote: Italians are opinion machines — “penso che”, “secondo me”, “credo che” open every debate from football to politics. The congiuntivo is your entry ticket.

lessons.title: Ne e ci: due piccole parole
lessons.objective: Use ne (of it/them) and ci (there / about it) like a native.
lessons.culturalNote: “Ci vediamo!” is how Italians say goodbye — literally “we will see each other (there)”. Ne and ci are the difference between textbook Italian and real Italian.

lessons.title: Che e cui: collegare le frasi
lessons.objective: Link sentences with the relative pronouns che and cui.
lessons.culturalNote: Elegant Italian loves long, linked sentences — newspapers and novels run on che and cui. Mastering them moves your Italian from short telegrams to real prose.

lessons.title: Stare + gerundio: azioni in corso
lessons.objective: Describe actions in progress with stare + gerundio.
lessons.culturalNote: “Sto arrivando!” (I’m on my way!) is the most useful phrase in Italian — usually said while still at home. Stare plus the gerundio is pure spoken Italian.

lessons.title: I comparativi
lessons.objective: Compare things with più/meno… di/che and the irregular forms.

legacyExercises.prompt: Il treno è ___ veloce dell’autobus. (faster)
legacyExercises.explanation: Comparing two things takes più… di. molto is just “very”; il più is the superlative; tanto needs quanto.

answers: La mia casa è più grande della tua.
legacyExercises.prompt: Type: My house is bigger than yours.
legacyExercises.explanation: più plus grande plus di: più grande della tua.

legacyExercises.prompt: Questo ristorante è ___ di quello. (better)
legacyExercises.explanation: buono gives migliore — an adjective, agreeing with ristorante. “più migliore” is a double comparative, wrong; meglio is the adverb.

answers: Questo computer è meno caro di quello.
legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order: This computer is less expensive than that one.
legacyExercises.explanation: meno plus the adjective plus di: Questo computer è meno caro di quello.

legacyExercises.prompt: Say it as an equality: È alto. (like me)
legacyExercises.explanation: Equality takes così… come — the così is often dropped: alto come me.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the comparison.
legacyExercises.explanation: Two coffees compared: più buono di — “more good than”.

answers: Perché è più leggero e migliore per il suo lavoro.
legacyExercises.prompt: Secondo il testo, perché ha scelto il secondo computer? (Why the second one?)
legacyExercises.explanation: “per il mio lavoro è migliore, perché viaggio molto” — lighter and better for travelling work.
legacyExercises.passage: Ho confrontato due computer. Il primo è più veloce e ha più memoria, ma è anche più caro. Il secondo è meno potente, però è più leggero e costa di meno. Alla fine ho scelto il secondo: per il mio lavoro è migliore, perché viaggio molto. A volte meno è meglio!
legacyExercises.translation: I compared two computers. The first is faster and has more memory, but it is also more expensive. The second is less powerful, but it is lighter and costs less. In the end I chose the second: for my work it is better, because I travel a lot. Sometimes less is more!

lessons.culturalNote: Italians compare everything — food, football teams, regions. “Il mio paese è più bello del tuo” starts friendly wars. Comparatives are social survival.

lessons.title: Il mondo del lavoro
lessons.objective: Talk about work with the si impersonale and key job vocabulary.
lessons.culturalNote: Job ads love the si impersonale — “si cerca”, “si richiede”, “si offre”. Reading annunci with si under your belt makes the whole job market legible.

lessons.title: Missione: una notte in albergo
lessons.objective: Check into a hotel, ask for what you need and solve a small problem — all in Italian.

lessons.title: Il passato prossimo con avere
lessons.objective: Talk about what you did yesterday using the passato prossimo with avere.
lessons.culturalNote: Italians love recounting their day in detail — raccontare la giornata is a national sport at the dinner table. The passato prossimo is your ticket into those conversations.

lessons.title: Il passato prossimo con essere
lessons.objective: Use essere as the helper for verbs of movement and change — with the participle that agrees.
lessons.culturalNote: Italian small talk runs on “dove sei andato in vacanza?” — where did you go on holiday. The essere past is the engine of every summer story.

lessons.title: L’imperfetto
lessons.objective: Describe habits and scenes from the past with the imperfetto.
lessons.culturalNote: “Quando ero piccolo…” (when I was little) opens a thousand Italian family stories. The imperfetto is how Italians do nostalgia.

lessons.title: Passato prossimo o imperfetto?
lessons.objective: Choose the right past tense — single events vs. background and habits — and tell the story of a day.
lessons.culturalNote: Raccontare la giornata — telling the story of your day — is sacred in Italy. Getting the two past tenses right is what makes your story sound Italian instead of translated.
